Research Proposal: Self-Specification Alignment for LLM-Generated Code##
Title
Self-Specification Alignment: Closing the Validation Loop for LLM Code
Generation Using Automatically Generated Behavioral Oracles

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
LLM-based code generation is evaluated almost entirely on observed test
coverage — does the generated code pass the few unit tests that ship with the
benchmark (HumanEval, MBPP, etc.)? This creates a well-known gap: code can pass
the provided tests while being functionally incorrect on edge cases or failing
to align with the full natural-language specification. In real software
engineering, the gap between "passes tests" and "correct" is where bugs live.

Current approaches (pass@k, test-time repair) attempt to close this gap by
sampling many candidates or brute-force re-prompting on test failure, but they
never broaden the test oracle itself. The specification is only consulted by the
human providing the original tests — the LLM never generates a specification it
then holds itself accountable to.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis> H1: For a given programming problem described in natural language,
an LLM can generate a behavioral oracle (a set of property-based or
example-based tests) that is more complete than the small set of tests provided
in the benchmark, and that oracle can be used to detect and repair incorrect
solutions that pass the original tests.

▌ H2: This self-specification + self-repair loop improves functional
▌ correctness over the baseline pass@k on the original test set, with
▌ diminishing returns bounded by the quality of the LLM-generated oracle.

The key claim is that the marginal correctness signal of self-generated tests —
tests the model writes about its own spec — is positive relative to the original
test set, even though the model generates both the code and the tests.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
The proposal consists of three stages:

Stage1 — Conditional Test GenerationGiven a problem description (docstring +
signature + examples), prompt the LLM to generate k additional test cases that:

• Cover edge cases (empty input, boundary values, large inputs, type
mismatches)
• Exercise postconditions stated in the docstring- Include both positive
(should pass) and negative (should reject/invalid input) casesConstraints:
the generated tests must be executable and self-contained.

Stage2 — Self-Specification ValidationFor each candidate solution:

1 Run it against the original benchmark tests. If it fails → discard.
2 Run it against the self-generated tests from Stage1. If it fails → flag for
repair.
3 Metric: oracle disagreement rate — what fraction of candidates that pass
original tests are caught by self-generated tests?

Stage3 — Iterative Self-RepairFor every candidate that passes original tests but
fails self-generated tests:

• Return the failing test(s) + failure message to the LLM as a repair prompt.
• Generate a repaired candidate.
• Re-validate against both original and self-generated tests.
• Repeat up to N iterations (or until all tests pass).
• Measure: success rate of repair (fraction of flagged candidates that pass all
tests after repair), and added correctness (fraction of originally-passed
problems that are now correct on a held-out test set).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark| Benchmark | Language | Problems | Relevance |

|---|---|---|---| | HumanEval+ (Liu et al.,2023) | Python |164 | Extended tests
beyond original HumanEval; serves as ground-truth oracle | | MBPP+ (Liu et
al.,2023) | Python |399 | Another standard; extended tests | | CodeContests
(DeepMind,2022) | Python/C++ | ~10k | Harder problems with rich test suites |

Use HumanEval+/MBPP+ as primary (known ground-truth oracles). The original test
set (5–10 tests) serves as the "provided tests"; the extended tests (Liu et
al.'s hand-audited additions or self-generated) serve as the evaluation oracle.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | Definition |

|---|---| | pass@k | Fraction of problems solved by any of k samples using
original tests | | self-gap | Fraction of pass@k solutions that fail
self-generated tests (oracle disagreement) | | repair recovery | Fraction of
self-gap failures that are repaired to pass all tests | | added-correctness@k |
Fraction of problems that only become correct after self-specification + repair
(true positives) | | over-repair rate | Fraction of problems where self-repair
breaks a previously correct solution (regression) | | test oracle precision |
Fraction of self-generated test failures that correspond to actual errors (on
held-out ground truth) |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines1. pass@k greedy — standard top-1 sampling, no repair.

2 pass@k sample — standard sampling (k=10,100,200).
3 self-repair (original tests only) — repair using only the original benchmark
tests (to isolate the value of additional self-generated tests).
4 LLM-as-judge (no execution) — ask the LLM whether the solution is correct,
without running tests; report as a soft ablation of the execution signal.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Ablations| Ablation | Question Answered |

|---|---| | No self-generated tests | Is the self-specification oracle adding
signal beyond just re-prompting? | | Self-generated tests from a different model
| Is the quality of self-generated tests model-dependent? (e.g., GPT-4o
generates tests, DeepSeek generates code) | | Single repair vs. multi-turn
repair | Does repair degrade after1–2 iterations (overfitting to generated
tests)? | | Docstring-only vs. docstring + signature + example | How much
specification context is needed to generate useful tests? | | Temperature
ablation on test generation | Does diverse test generation (high T) improve
oracle coverage? |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes1. Circular validation — The LLM generates tests that
match its code bugs instead of the spec. If both code and tests share the same
blind spot, the oracle adds no signal → large self-gap is actually large
false-negative rate. Mitigation: measure precision on human-audited extended
tests (HumanEval+).

2 Over-repair / regressions — Repairing against self-generated tests breaks
correctness on the original tests or introduces new bugs. Mitigation: always
check original tests post-repair; report over-repair rate explicitly.
3 Specification underspecification — The docstring itself is ambiguous or
underspecified, so no amount of test generation can disambiguate it. The
method is bounded by the quality of the input specification. Mitigation:
filter problems where human annotators deem the spec unambiguous and report
results conditioned on specification clarity.
4 Test generation cost — Generating k test cases per problem × n samples ×
repair iterations is significantly more expensive than sampling alone.
Mitigation: report token cost per solved problem; treat this as a proposed
quality-cost tradeoff.
5 Model self-attribution bias — The model may be overly agreeable with its own
generated tests, failing to challenge its code against rigorous oracles. The
cross-model ablation (tests from model A, code from model B) tests this
directly.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Proposed Experimental Protocol1. For each problem, generate self-specification
tests (k=20) from the docstring.

2 Draw100 code samples per problem (pass@k evaluation).
3 For each sample passing original tests: run self-generated tests; flag
failures.
4 Attempt repair (up to3 iterations) on each flagged candidate.
5 Evaluate final correctness against HumanEval+ extended tests (ground truth).
6 Report: pass@k (baseline), added-correctness (method), self-gap, repair
recovery, over-repair rate, token cost per problem.

**1. Title**
Graph-Augmented Multi-Agent Refactoring (GAMAR): Reducing Global Technical Debt through Structured Dependency Context.

**2. Problem and Motivation**
Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at local code completion but struggle with "global" software engineering tasks like refactoring "God Objects" or decoupling circular dependencies. The primary bottleneck is the "lost-in-the-middle" phenomenon and context window limitations, where models lose track of distant call-site dependencies. Current AI tools often introduce regressions because they lack a holistic understanding of the codebase's architectural constraints, leading to a "hallucination of local correctness" that breaks global system integrity.

**3. Core Hypothesis**
Integrating a static-analysis-derived Code Property Graph (CPG) into a multi-agent feedback loop—consisting of an Architect agent (planning), a Coder agent (implementation), and a Verifier agent (validation)—will result in a higher reduction of Cyclomatic Complexity and higher unit test pass rates compared to monolithic, zero-shot LLM refactoring.

**4. Method**
1.  **Graph Extraction:** Use *Joern* or *Tree-sitter* to generate a CPG of the target repository, capturing Abstract Syntax Trees (AST), Control Flow Graphs (CFG), and Program Dependence Graphs (PDG).
2.  **Architect Agent:** Given a high-complexity module (identified via static metrics), the Architect queries the CPG to identify all incoming/outgoing dependencies and proposes a refactoring plan (e.g., Extract Class, Move Method).
3.  **Coder Agent:** Executes the plan by modifying specific files. It uses the CPG to identify exactly which call sites require signature updates.
4.  **Verifier Agent:** Triggers a dual-validation pipeline: (a) Static check via the CPG to ensure no broken references; (b) Dynamic check via existing test suites.
5.  **Iteration:** If validation fails, the error logs are fed back to the Architect to revise the plan.

**5. Dataset or Benchmark**
*   **Refactoring-Critic:** A dataset of human-verified refactorings.
*   **Defects4J (selected subsets):** Specifically the modules with high technical debt metrics.
*   **Project-Level Repositories:** 50 high-star Java and Python repositories from GitHub with documented "Code Smells" (identified via *SonarQube*).

**6. Evaluation Metrics**
*   **Structural Metrics:** Reduction in Cyclomatic Complexity (CC) and Halstead Complexity.
*   **Correctness:** Pass@k for existing unit tests post-refactor.
*   **Maintainability Index (MI):** Pre- vs. post-refactoring score.
*   **Dependency Impact:** Number of unintended side effects (broken external calls) caught by the Verifier.

**7. Baselines**
*   **Zero-shot GPT-4:** Providing the entire module code with a "refactor this" prompt.
*   **RAG-based LLM:** Retrieving relevant code snippets via vector similarity (ChromaDB/Pinecone) rather than a structured graph.
*   **Traditional Static Analysis Tools:** Automated refactoring features in IDEs like IntelliJ IDEA or Eclipse.

**8. Ablations**
*   **Graph vs. Text:** Remove the CPG and provide only raw file text to the agents.
*   **Multi-Agent vs. Single-Agent:** Collapse the Architect, Coder, and Verifier into a single prompt session.
*   **Feedback Loop:** Remove the Verifier's ability to trigger re-planning (one-pass generation).

**9. Failure Modes and Feasibility Risks**
*   **Graph Scaling:** For repositories >1M LOC, the CPG may exceed memory limits or become too dense for the LLM to parse efficiently.
*   **Tooling Fragility:** Static analysis tools (Joern) may fail on non-standard syntax or multi-language interop.
*   **Token Consumption:** Multi-agent iterations on large files can become prohibitively expensive; mitigation involves using "diff-only" prompting to minimize context.
*   **Test Coverage:** If the original repo has low test coverage, the Verifier cannot guarantee functional equivalence, leading to "silent regressions."

Research Proposal: Addressing Accuracy Issues in Automated LLM Evaluation---

Title
Calibrated Ensemble Evaluation (CEE): Improving LLM-as-a-Judge Accuracy
through Uncertainty-Aware Multi-Model Deliberation

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
LLM-based automated evaluators ("LLM-as-a-judge") are the dominant method
for evaluating open-ended text generation at scale, but suffer from four
well-documented accuracy issues:

1 Systematic biases — position bias (preferring first or second response),
verbosity bias (preferring longer outputs), and self-enhancement bias
(preferring outputs from models similar to the judge).
2 No uncertainty quantification — standard practice returns a point estimate
(score or preference) with no confidence, making it impossible to know when
the judge is uncertain vs confident.
3 Low inter-rater reliability — agreement between LLM judges and human raters
varies wildly across domains (Spearman ρ ranges from0.3 on creative writing
to0.7 on factual QA).
4 Rubric brittleness — even with detailed rubrics, LLM judges often fail to
follow multi-criteria instructions consistently, collapsing dimensions or
ignoring criteria.

The core unmet need is an evaluation framework that produces trustworthy scores
— scores that are calibrated, debiased, and accompanied by uncertainty — rather
than simply fast scores.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
Decomposing evaluation into atomic quality criteria, aggregating
judgments from multiple diverse evaluator LLMs with explicit uncertainty
estimation, and calibrating the resulting scores against a small human-annotated
set will significantly improve accuracy — defined as Spearman rank correlation
with held-out human judgments — over the standard single-model, single-pass,
holistic-judgment baseline, while also reducing known biases (position,
verbosity) and providing well-calibrated uncertainty estimates.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method (3-stage pipeline)

Stage1: Atomic Criterion DecompositionInstead of asking a judge for a single
"overall quality" score (which collapses heterogeneous dimensions), decompose
evaluation into6 atomic rubrics:

#  Criterion              Definition
1  Relevance              Does the response address the prompt directly?
2  Correctness            Are factual claims accurate? (for knowledge tasks)
3  Coherence              Is the response logically structured and internally
consistent?
4  Completeness           Does the response cover the scope requested?
5  Conciseness            Is the response free of unnecessary verbosity?
6  Instruction Following  Does the response obey format, length, and style
constraints?

Each criterion is scored on a1–5 Likert scale by each evaluator model, using a
criterion-specific prompt that includes the rubric definition, the prompt, and
the response. This prevents any single criterion from dominating.

Stage2: Multi-Model Panel with UncertaintyQuery a panel of K =3 to5 diverse LLM
evaluators (from different model families, e.g., GPT-4o, Claude3.5 Sonnet,
Llama370B, Gemini2.0 Flash, Mistral Large). Each model scores each response on
all6 criteria.

For each (model, criterion, response) triple, also extract the log-probability
of the score token(s) as a proxy for the model's confidence in that judgment.
This gives a per-criterion confidence weight.

Stage3: Calibration LayerUsing a held-out calibration set of N =500–1,000
examples with human ratings on the same6 criteria (collected from3 annotators
per example):

1 Score Aggregation: Per criterion, compute a confidence-weighted average
across models: s_c = Σ_i w_i_c * score_i_c / Σ_i w_i_c where w_i_c =
exp(logprob_i_c) is model i's confidence on criterion c.
2 Bias Correction: Fit a small logistic regression or isotonic regression per
criterion to map the aggregated score s_c to a calibrated score ŝ_c that
minimizes expected calibration error against human ratings.
3 Uncertainty Output: For each response, output both the calibrated score
vector ŝ ∈ [1,5]^6 and a per-criterion uncertainty interval derived from the
weighted variance across the panel.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark| Dataset | Use | Size | Human Annotations |

|---------|-----|------|-------------------| | MT-Bench | Primary evaluation |80
multi-turn questions,3,360 model outputs | Human preference + pairwise ratings
(published) | | Chatbot Arena (subset) | Primary evaluation |10K randomly
sampled comparisons | Human preference votes (public) | | FLASK | Fine-grained
evaluation | ~1,700 model outputs | Human ratings on12 fine-grained dimensions |
| ShareGPT + rubric annotation | Calibration set |500 examples,3 annotators/ex |
Collected fresh (6 atomic criteria + overall) | | AlpacaEval2.0 | OOD test |805
examples | Length-controlled win rates (indirect human signal) |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | What it measures | Target |

|--------|-----------------|--------| | Spearman ρ (with human scores) | Rank
correlation — primary metric | >0.65 (vs ~0.50–0.55 for GPT-4 baseline on
creative/ open-ended tasks) | | Exact + Adjacent Agreement | Score-level match
with humans | >60% exact +85% adjacent | | Position Bias Rate | % of trials
where swapping A/B order flips the preference | <5% (vs ~15–20% for single-model
judges) | | Verbosity Correlation | Pearson r between predicted score and
response length (log tokens) | |r| <0.10 (vs ~0.35 for rubric-free judges) | |
Expected Calibration Error (ECE) | Binned calibration of confidence vs accuracy
| <0.08 | | Test-Retest Consistency | Variance across3 independent runs on same
input | σ² <0.02 per criterion | | Cost per Evaluation | API cost per evaluation
@ inference time | Report in USD for transparency |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines| Baseline | Description | Why chosen |

|----------|-------------|------------| | GPT-4-as-a-judge (holistic) | Single
GPT-4 call scoring "overall quality"1–5 | De facto standard in most LLM
evaluation pipelines | | GPT-4-as-a-judge (with rubric) | Same model, but with
the6 atomic criteria in prompt | Controls for rubric decomposition effect alone
| | PairRM | Trained pairwise reward model (based on Llama) | Representative of
trained, task-specific evaluators | | JudgeLM | Fine-tuned evaluator on100K
human judgments | Strongest published fine-tuned baseline | | Majority Vote (3x)
| Same model (GPT-4) called3 times, majority vote | Controls for the effect of
repeated sampling alone | | Humans (held out) | Human judgment on held-out test
set | Upper-bound oracle (no automated evaluation is expected to match this, but
it anchors the comparison) |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Ablations
Each ablation removes or varies one component of CEE while holding
everything else fixed, tested on the MT-Bench test set:

Ablation                 Variation                  What it isolates
Panel size               K =1 vs3 vs5 models        Value of model diversity
Criterion decomposition  Replace6 criteria with     Value of atomic rubric
single holistic "overall"  structure
judgment
Uncertainty weighting    Replace                    Value of log-prob
confidence-weighted        confidence signal
average with uniform
average
Calibration layer        Remove calibration (use    Value of human-anchored
raw aggregated scores)     calibration
Model diversity          Same-family panel (GPT-4o  Value of cross-family
×3) vs cross-family        diversity vs repeated
(GPT-4o + Claude + Llama)  sampling

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes| Failure Mode | Likelihood | Mitigation |

|-------------|-----------|------------| | Calibration overfitting — the
calibration layer overfits to the small (500-example) human set and degrades on
OOD distributions like AlpacaEval | Medium | Use regularization (isotonic
regression with smoothing); report OOD performance separately; scale calibration
set to1,000 if budget permits | | Model collinearity — diverse models produce
correlated errors on the same failure cases (e.g., all miss subtle factual
errors in stylized text) | Medium-High | Analyze error correlation matrix across
models; if collinearity is high (>0.8 across all pairs), consider subsampling to
the two most independent models | | Criterion decomposition misses holistic
qualities — atomic rubrics fail to capture emergent dimensions (interestingness,
novelty, tone) that drive human preferences | Medium | Add a7th "overall
gestalt" criterion alongside atomic ones; check whether the holistic dimension
is needed for high human correlation via ablation | | Computational cost — K ×6
API calls per evaluation (e.g.,5 ×6 =30 calls) is15–30× more expensive than a
single-judge baseline, limiting practical adoption | High | Accept cost as a
trade-off for research-phase accuracy; report cost per evaluation; investigate
whether pruning to the top-2 criteria after a pilot study can reduce calls3×
with minimal accuracy loss | | Rubric leakage — models exhibit new
criterion-specific biases (e.g., always giving "conciseness" low scores to long
but good answers) | Medium | Exploratory analysis of per-criterion score
distributions; adjust rubric wording in a small pilot (N=50) before finalizing |
| Human annotation bottleneck — collecting500 ×6 ×3 ≈9,000 reliable
atomic-criterion annotations is expensive and slow | High | Use existing FLASK
dataset (already has fine-grained annotations) to bootstrap; only collect ~200
fresh annotations for the calibration held-out set | | Log-prob confidence is
poorly calibrated — score-token log-probs may not reflect true judgment
confidence, especially under sampling temperature >0 | Medium | Set temperature
to0 for evaluation calls; if log-probs still unreliable, replace with
self-reported confidence ("How confident are you in this score on a1-5 scale?")
as an alternative confidence signal |

**1. Title**
Meta-Evaluative Deliberation: Reducing LLM-as-a-Judge Bias via Attribution-Anchored Multi-Agent Consensus.

**2. Problem and Motivation**
Current automated evaluation frameworks (e.g., LLM-as-a-judge) exhibit significant systematic biases, including position bias (preferring the first presented candidate), verbosity bias (preferring longer outputs regardless of quality), and self-preference bias. Furthermore, evaluators often suffer from "hallucinated grading," where the judge rewards factually incorrect responses that appear stylistically confident. As LLMs are increasingly used to train reward models (RLHF), inaccuracies in evaluation lead to reward hacking and model degradation.

**3. Core Hypothesis**
Decomposing the evaluation process into an "Atomic Fact Verification" phase followed by a "Multi-Agent Deliberation" phase will increase the Spearman correlation with human expert judgments by at least 15% compared to single-pass zero-shot prompting (e.g., GPT-4 Turbo). Specifically, anchoring the final score to verified claims mitigates verbosity bias.

**4. Method**
*   **Step 1: Atomic Claim Extraction:** Use a fine-tuned Llama-3-70B to decompose the candidate response into a list of checkable atomic claims.
*   **Step 2: External/Reference Grounding:** Verify each claim against the provided reference context or a retrieved knowledge snippet using a Natural Language Inference (NLI) model (e.g., DeBERTa-v3-large).
*   **Step 3: Multi-Agent Debate (MAD):** Deploy three specialized agent roles:
    *   *The Fact-Checker:* Penalizes hallucinations based on Step 2.
    *   *The Stylist:* Evaluates coherence, tone, and formatting.
    *   *The Moderator:* Synthesizes the two perspectives into a final Likert scale (1-5) or pairwise ranking.
*   **Step 4: Self-Reflective Calibration:** The moderator must provide a "confidence score" based on the internal consistency of the debate. If confidence is low, the system triggers a second round of deliberation with shuffled input order to neutralize position bias.

**5. Dataset or Benchmark**
*   **AlpacaEval 2.0:** For testing head-to-head win rates against a reference model.
*   **MT-Bench:** For multi-turn conversation evaluation.
*   **RewardBench:** To specifically evaluate the judge's ability to distinguish between subtle reasoning errors and correct logic.

**6. Evaluation Metrics**
*   **Spearman’s $\rho$ and Kendall’s $\tau$:** Correlation between the automated scores and human-annotated ground truth.
*   **Systematic Bias Coefficients:** Measuring the variance in scores when input order is swapped (Position Bias) or when filler text is added (Verbosity Bias).
*   **Human Agreement Rate:** Percentage of ties broken by the system that match human expert preferences.

**7. Baselines**
*   **GPT-4 (Zero-shot):** The standard "LLM-as-a-judge" configuration.
*   **G-Eval:** A Chain-of-Thought (CoT) based evaluation framework.
*   **Prometheus-2:** An open-source evaluator model trained specifically for feedback generation.

**8. Ablations**
*   **-Attribution:** Removing the NLI-based fact-checking step to measure the impact of grounding.
*   **-Multi-Agent:** Running the same prompt through a single agent to measure the impact of deliberation.
*   **-Shuffle:** Removing the position-swapping step to quantify the baseline position bias of the moderator.

**9. Failure Modes and Feasibility Risks**
*   **Inference Latency:** The multi-agent and multi-step process significantly increases the token cost and wall-clock time per evaluation.
*   **Consensus Collapse:** In complex reasoning tasks, agents may converge on a "majority-incorrect" opinion if the underlying base models share the same training data biases.
*   **NLI Sensitivity:** If the Atomic Claim Extraction is too granular, the NLI model may produce excessive false negatives, leading to overly harsh grading.

Research Proposal: Multi-Agent LLM Systems for Clinical Trial Eligibility
Screening## Title
TrialMatch: A Structured Multi-Agent Debate Framework for
Zero-Shot Clinical Trial Eligibility Screening

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Clinical trial enrollment is the bottleneck of medical research.
Eligibility screening — determining whether a patient's unstructured EHR notes
satisfy a trial's inclusion/exclusion criteria — is currently performed manually
by coordinators. This is slow, error-prone, and does not scale to the ~400,000
trials on ClinicalTrials.gov.

Single-pass LLM prompting achieves ~70–75% F1 on eligibility classification
(TrialGPT,2024), but suffers from two issues: (a) it hallucinates criterion
matches for ambiguous or missing data, and (b) it does not handle contradictory
criteria across multiple trials for the same patient.

Open question: Can a multi-agent debate architecture, where specialized agents
argue for and against each criterion, outperform a single monolithic LLM on this
task?

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
A multi-agent debate system — where one agent argues for criterion
satisfaction (citing specific evidence), a second argues against, and a judge
agent synthesizes the final decision — will improve F1 by ≥5 points over a
single-pass LLM with equal total inference cost, because forced adversarial
reasoning reduces hallucination on borderline criteria.

Null hypothesis: Multi-agent debate does not significantly outperform
single-pass prompting when both use the same backbone LLM and comparable token
budgets.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
### Architecture: TrialMatchThe system operates in three stages per
patient-trial pair:

1 Evidence Extraction: An extractor agent reads the patient note + trial
criteria and produces a structured table mapping each criterion to the spans
of text that are relevant (or marks the criterion as "no evidence in note").
2 Adversarial Debate (per criterion):

• Pro Agent — given the criterion and extracted evidence, argues why the
patient meets this criterion.
• Con Agent — given the same evidence, argues why the patient does not meet it.
• Each agent is temperature-decayed (T=0.7 →0.3) over3 rounds; they see each
other's arguments.

3 Aggregation & Prediction:

• Judge Agent — reads the debate transcripts for all criteria and produces:
• A binary eligibility decision (eligible / ineligible)
• A confidence score - Citations to specific spans in the original
noteBackbone: Llama-3.1-70B (or a similarly capable open model), quantized to
allow multi-agent rollouts on a single A100.

Prompt structure: Each agent is prompted with a role persona (e.g., "You are a
conservative clinical reviewer who requires explicit documentation before
approving") to ensure separation of perspectives.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark
Primary: TrialGPT benchmark (Jin et al.,2024) —183 patient
summaries (from TREC Clinical Trials) and3,500+ trial-criterion pairs with
expert-annotated eligibility labels. This is the standard zero-shot benchmark.

Secondary (robustness): N2C22018 (Adverse Drug Events cohort) — convert the ADE
extraction task into criterion-style screening for a drug trial; measure
cross-dataset transfer.

Validation method:5-fold patient-level cross-validation on TrialGPT. No patient
appears in both train and test folds.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | Rationale |

|---|---| | Macro F1 (primary) | Balanced measure for binary eligibility;
primary metric in TrialGPT | | Criterion-level accuracy | Per-criterion match vs
annotator labels (from TrialGPT's fine-grained labels) | | Precision vs Recall
tradeoff | Important for clinical use — false positives (enrolling an ineligible
patient) are costlier than false negatives | | Mean confidence calibration (ECE)
| Judge confidence should correlate with correctness | | Debate round
convergence | Does additional debate rounds (>3) change the final decision?
(sensitivity analysis) | | Token cost | Total tokens consumed per patient-trial
pair (runtime cost matters for deployment) |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines1. Single-pass LLM (same backbone, same evidence extraction step, no
debate) — direct ablation2. TrialGPT (Jin et al.,2024) — strongest published
zero-shot baseline3. Chain-of-Thought prompting on the same backbone — controls
for reasoning depth4. Self-consistency (Wang et al.,2023) with5 samples —
controls for ensemble effect vs. structured debate5. Random majority (predict
the majority class per trial) — sanity floorAll baselines share the same
evidence extraction stage and backbone model for fair comparison.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Ablations1. No debate → single-pass LLM (this is baseline1 above)

2 Single-agent self-consistency (same number of forward passes as debate, but
no adversarial structure) — isolates the benefit of adversarial reasoning vs.
mere sampling3. Judge only, no pro/con (judge sees evidence directly) —
isolates the value of debate4. Debate without role personas (both agents
prompted as neutral reviewers) — tests whether forced role separation
matters5. Temperature ablation (fixed high vs. fixed low vs. decay schedule)
3 Backbone size (8B vs.70B) — does debate help smaller models more?

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes| Failure Mode | Mitigation |

|---|---| | Both pro and con hallucinate — debate converges on wrong facts
because both agents invent evidence | Evidence extraction stage is constrained
to quote spans only; agents cannot fabricate new facts | | Judge favors
pro/consistently — positional bias or role bias in the judge | Swap agent order
randomly; test two judge prompts (neutral; "prefer inclusion"; "prefer
exclusion") | | Token cost is prohibitive — multi-agent debate uses3–5× more
tokens than single-pass | Measure cost explicitly; report F1 per token. If gain
is <5 points, single-pass is economically preferable | | No improvement on easy
criteria — debate only helps borderline cases, which are rare (~15% of criteria)
| Report separately on "easy" (both agents initially agree) vs "hard" criteria;
overall F1 gain may be diluted | | Agent personas polarize unrecoverably — pro
and con become entrenched and never converge | Hard-limit at3 rounds; judge
always has the final say regardless of agreement | | Dataset leakage — LLM was
pre-trained on ClinicalTrials.gov or MIMIC notes | Use a held-out set of recent
trials (past12 months, beyond training cutoff); check for exact matches | |
Cross-dataset transfer fails — N2C2 performance is at or below random | Accept
as a limitation; report honestly. Consider fine-tuning the evidence extraction
stage on N2C2 |

**1. Title**
Hierarchical Multi-Agent Refinement for Guideline-Adherent Differential Diagnosis (H-MARD)

**2. Problem and Motivation**
Large Language Models (LLMs) in clinical settings frequently exhibit "premature closure"—the tendency to jump to a diagnosis without exhaustive consideration of alternative hypotheses or adherence to established clinical pathways (e.g., ordering high-cost imaging before bedside exams). While single-turn RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) improves factual recall, it fails to enforce the sequential logic required by clinical guidelines (e.g., GOLD for COPD or AHA for hypertension). There is a critical need for agentic architectures that decouple hypothesis generation from clinical verification.

**3. Core Hypothesis**
A hierarchical multi-agent system—comprising a "Diagnostic Proposer" and a "Guideline Critic" grounded in medical ontologies—will achieve higher diagnostic accuracy and better adherence to clinical protocols than single-agent systems by forcing explicit verification of intermediate diagnostic steps.

**4. Method**
The H-MARD framework employs two specialized agents:
*   **The Proposer Agent:** Generates a differential diagnosis (DDx) and a proposed workup using Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting.
*   **The Critic Agent:** Utilizes a RAG pipeline indexed over clinical textbooks (e.g., Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine) and a Knowledge Graph (UMLS) to audit the Proposer’s output.
*   **The Loop:** If the Critic identifies a guideline violation (e.g., "MRI suggested before X-ray for suspected osteoarthritis"), it returns a structured critique. The Proposer must then regenerate the plan. This continues for a maximum of $N=3$ iterations or until the Critic issues a "Pass" token.

**5. Dataset or Benchmark**
*   **MedQA (USMLE):** For evaluating standardized medical knowledge and reasoning.
*   **MIMIC-IV-ED:** De-identified electronic health records from emergency departments to test reasoning on real-world, noisy clinical trajectories.
*   **DDxPlus:** A large-scale dataset specifically designed for differential diagnosis with symptom-disease links.

**6. Evaluation Metrics**
*   **Diagnostic Accuracy (Top-1 and Top-3):** Correctness of the final diagnosis.
*   **Guideline Adherence Score (GAS):** A custom metric measuring the percentage of suggested diagnostic steps that align with standard-of-care sequences (evaluated via expert-annotated templates).
*   **Test Parsimony:** The ratio of "necessary" to "redundant" diagnostic tests suggested.
*   **UMLS Grounding Ratio:** The percentage of generated medical entities successfully mapped to UMLS Concept Unique Identifiers (CUIs).

**7. Baselines**
*   **Zero-shot LLMs:** GPT-4o and Llama-3-70B-Instruct.
*   **Med-PaLM 2 (or open-source equivalent like Med-Llama-3):** Domain-specific fine-tuned models.
*   **Standard RAG:** A single-agent system with access to the same clinical corpus but without the iterative critic loop.

**8. Ablations**
*   **No Critic:** Removing the Verifier agent to test the impact of the feedback loop.
*   **No RAG:** The Critic relies on its internal weights rather than external clinical guidelines.
*   **Zero Feedback:** The Critic provides a score but no textual feedback for refinement.

**9. Failure Modes and Feasibility Risks**
*   **Infinite Loop/Oscillation:** The Proposer and Critic may enter a non-convergent cycle where they disagree indefinitely on subjective presentations.
*   **Knowledge Conflict:** Discrepancies between different clinical guidelines (e.g., ACC vs. ESC) may confuse the Critic agent.
*   **Latency:** The multi-agent iterative process significantly increases inference time and API costs compared to single-turn generation.
*   **Hallucinated Guidelines:** The Critic may fabricate a "protocol" that does not exist if the RAG retrieval fails to find a relevant document.

Title: Structured Critical Literature Review Generation via Hierarchical
Contradiction-Aware Synthesis---

Problem
Current automated literature review systems (LLM-based or
retrieval-augmented) produce fluent but shallow summaries — they list findings
paper-by-paper, avoid conflicting results, and fail to organize knowledge into
the canonical sub-topics, debates, and open questions a human reviewer would
surface. No existing system explicitly models contradictions across papers or
generates a structured review with sections like "consensus findings,"
"conflicting evidence," and "methodological gaps."

Hypothesis
A hierarchical, contradiction-aware pipeline that (1) retrieves and
clusters papers by sub-topic, (2) extracts claim-level triples (method, finding,
direction of effect), and (3) explicitly identifies and resolves or flags
contradictions, will produce literature reviews that are rated by domain experts
as more organized, more critical, and more useful than retrieval-augmented
baselines that only summarize per-paper or per-topic.

Method
Stage1 — Hierarchical topic structuring. Given a query (e.g.
"chain-of-thought reasoning"), query a paper corpus (e.g. S2ORC / Semantic
Scholar) and cluster retrieved abstracts using a hierarchical embedding +
LLM-labeling pipeline (HDBSCAN on SBERT embeddings, then GPT-4o-mini assigns
canonical section headings).

Stage2 — Claim extraction and contradiction detection. For each paper, extract
structured claim triples (entity, predicate, direction/sign) via a fine-tuned
DeBERTa-v3 or prompted LLM. Within each sub-topic cluster, compare claim triples
for directional mismatches (e.g. "CoT improves accuracy on GSM8K" vs "CoT does
not improve accuracy on GSM8K"). Flag contradictions with supporting citations
on both sides.

Stage3 — Contradiction-aware synthesis. Generate the review section-by-section
using a controlled generation loop: (a) draft a section from the consensus
claims, (b) conditionally append a "conflicting evidence" sub-section if
contradictions were detected, (c) append an "open questions" sub-section
identifying gaps where evidence is absent or contradictory.

Stage4 — Citation grounding and fact verification. Each generated claim is
back-linked to the original source passage. A lightweight fact-verification step
(NLI-based, e.g. TrueTeacher) verifies whether the generated claim is entailed
by the cited passage. Unverifiable claims are removed or softened.

Dataset / Benchmark- Corpus: Semantic Scholar Open Research Corpus (S2ORC) — ~8M
papers, with full text when available. Restrict to4-5 well-surveyed domains
(e.g., LLM reasoning, protein folding, adversarial robustness, representation
learning, NLP for low-resource languages).

• Gold-standard reviews: For each domain, collect2-3 human-written survey
papers (e.g. from arXiv, JMLR, ACL anthology). Segment into sections as
ground-truth structure.
• Review quality evaluation set: Construct50 query-review pairs per domain,
each with3 expert ratings along organization, coverage, critical depth, and
usefulness (1–5 Likert).

Evaluation Metrics| Dimension | Metric | How measured |

|---|---|---| | Structure | Section overlap (ROUGE-L / Jaccard on section
headings) | Against human survey TOC | | Coverage | Recall of cited papers from
human survey reference list | Macro-averaged per section | | Critical depth |
Contradiction recall — fraction of known conflicting findings surfaced |
Hand-labeled conflict set | | Faithfulness | % of claims entailed by cited
passages | NLI-based verification + human spot-check | | Overall quality |
Expert rating (1–5) on organization, usefulness | Blind rating by3 domain
experts |

Baselines1. Naive RAG — Retrieve top-20 papers, concatenate abstracts, prompt
GPT-4o to write a review.

2 Per-paper summarization — Summarize each paper individually, then concatenate
under LLM-generated headings (Liu et al.,2024-style).
3 Topic-cluster summarization — Cluster papers by topic, summarize cluster,
then synthesize (similar to Scim,2024).
4 Ours w/o contradiction detection — Same pipeline but skip Stage2
contradiction flagging (ablate the core mechanism).

Ablations- A1: Remove hierarchical clustering → flat topic list (tests whether
hierarchy improves organization).

• A2: Remove fact-verification filter (tests whether filtering reduces
hallucination at the cost of coverage).
• A3: Replace GPT-4o claim extraction with fine-tuned DeBERTa-v3 (tests whether
a smaller model suffices).
• A4: Remove contradiction-aware sub-section generation → always write
consensus-only text (tests the value of explicit contradiction flagging vs.
implicit handling).

Expected Failure Modes1. Contradictions are rare or subtle. Most papers in a
well-matured field may agree on fundamentals, leaving little for the
contradiction module to surface. Mitigation: evaluate on at least one rapidly
evolving domain (e.g., LLM reasoning post-2023) where disagreements are common.

2 Claim extraction noise propagates. A false-positive contradiction (two claims
that appear contradictory but differ in experimental setup) degrades the
review. Mitigation: require supporting citations on both sides; add a
confidence threshold for contradiction flagging.
3 Expert raters prefer concise over critical. Human readers may rate a fluent,
uncontroversial summary higher than one that honestly reports messy
disagreements. Mitigation: structure expert evaluation to score critical
depth and usefulness separately from fluency and organization.
4 Structure diversity across human surveys. Two human surveys on the same topic
often use different section taxonomies, making section-overlap metrics noisy.
Mitigation: use macro-averaged ROUGE-L and report variance; also report
expert agreement (Fleiss' κ) on organization.
5 Domain shift. A pipeline tuned on NLP papers may fail for biomedical or
physics literature where citation practices and claim phrasing differ.
Mitigation: hold out one domain for final evaluation only, to measure
generalization.

### 1. Title
Hierarchical Graph-Augmented Synthesis (HGAS): Leveraging Citation Topology for Thematic Literature Review Generation.

### 2. Problem and Motivation
Current automated literature review (LR) systems predominantly use flat Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), which often results in "serial summarization"—a sequence of isolated paper summaries rather than a synthesized thematic narrative. These systems struggle with global coherence, redundant information across overlapping papers, and a failure to capture the evolution of research trajectories. Effective LRs require identifying the latent conceptual structure of a field, which is often encoded in the citation graph and semantic clusters rather than individual abstracts.

### 3. Core Hypothesis
By explicitly modeling the citation graph and performing community detection (e.g., Leiden algorithm) on the document embedding space, a hierarchical planning module can generate a more coherent and less redundant synthesis than standard top-k retrieval methods.

### 4. Method
The HGAS framework consists of four stages:
1.  **Graph-Based Retrieval:** Given a query, retrieve a candidate set $P$ (e.g., $n=100$) using hybrid search (BM25 + Specter2 embeddings). Construct a local citation subgraph where edges represent direct citations or co-citation patterns.
2.  **Thematic Clustering:** Apply the Leiden community detection algorithm on the subgraph to identify $k$ thematic clusters. For each cluster, extract key phrases using TextRank to define "Sub-topic Centroids."
3.  **Hierarchical Planning:** An LLM (e.g., GPT-4o) generates a structured outline where each section corresponds to a cluster. The order is determined by a temporal-logical flow (e.g., foundational papers first, followed by specialized branches).
4.  **Iterative Synthesis:** Generate text for each section using a "sliding window of context" where the LLM is provided with the current cluster's full text, the summary of previous sections, and a "contrastive prompt" to highlight differences between the current cluster and previous ones.

### 5. Dataset or Benchmark
*   **S2ORC (Semantic Scholar Open Research Corpus):** Specifically the "Computer Science" and "Medicine" subsets for high-density citation data.
*   **Multi-XScience:** A large-scale dataset for multi-document summarization of scientific articles.
*   **Delphi-Review:** A curated set of 500 human-written survey papers paired with their primary references for ground-truth comparison.

### 6. Evaluation Metrics
*   **Synthesis Score:** A custom metric calculating the ratio of multi-citation sentences to single-citation sentences.
*   **Entity Coverage:** Recall of key technical entities (identified via SciSpacy) from the reference set.
*   **Coherence (Entity Grid):** Using the Barzilay-Lapata entity grid model to measure local transitions.
*   **ROUGE-L & BERTScore:** To measure overlap with human-written survey abstracts.

### 7. Baselines
*   **Naive RAG:** Standard top-k retrieval with long-context window (e.g., Claude 3.5 Sonnet).
*   **Re-Ranker RAG:** Using a cross-encoder to re-rank the top 20 papers before generation.
*   **SurveyAgent:** A recent agentic baseline that uses iterative searching but lacks graph-based clustering.

### 8. Ablations
*   **No-Graph:** Perform clustering based only on semantic embeddings (Cosine similarity) without citation edges.
*   **No-Planning:** Generate the review in a single pass without the hierarchical outline.
*   **Random Ordering:** Provide clusters to the generator in a shuffled order to test the importance of the temporal-logical flow.

### 9. Failure Modes and Feasibility Risks
*   **Graph Sparsity:** In emerging or niche fields, citation edges may be too sparse for effective community detection. *Mitigation:* Fall back to semantic similarity clustering.
*   **Context Window Limits:** Even with long-context LLMs, feeding full-text for 50+ papers is computationally expensive. *Mitigation:* Use extractive summarization on individual papers before the synthesis stage.
*   **Hallucination of Connections:** The model may claim Paper A builds on Paper B when they are merely contemporaneous. *Mitigation:* Explicitly prompt the model to verify citation directionality using the graph metadata.

answer_a_text:
Research Proposal: Confidence-Gated Iterative Pseudo-Labeling with
Phoneme-Constrained Augmentation for Low-Resource ASRTitle: Semi-Supervised
Self-Training with Audited Pseudo-Labels and Phoneme-Preserving Augmentation for
Under-10-Hour Speech Recognition---

Problem
State-of-the-art ASR systems (e.g., Whisper, wav2vec2.0) degrade
catastrophically when fine-tuned on fewer than10 hours of transcribed speech.
Two failure modes dominate: (1) overfitting to the small labeled set, and (2)
confirmation bias in self-training, where the model reinforces its own errors
through noisy pseudo-labels on unlabeled data. No existing method jointly
addresses label quality and data diversity in the under-10-hour regime on a
single pipeline.

Hypothesis
A self-training loop that audits pseudo-labels through a separate
confidence calibrator (rather than the ASR model's own softmax) and couples them
with phoneme-preserving augmentations (time-stretch, pitch-shift, and speed
perturbation clipped to per-phoneme duration bounds) will outperform standard
pseudo-labeling and unsupervised pre-training when labeled data ≤10 hours. The
key claim: auditing prevents confirmation bias, and phoneme-constrained
augmentation prevents the augmentations from destroying linguistic content that
the small labeled set cannot recover.

Method1. Seed model — Fine-tune a small SSL encoder (wav2vec2.0 Base, ~95M
params) on the labeled set (≤10 h). Use a single linear projection head.

2 Pseudo-labeling loop (3 rounds):

• Decode the unlabeled pool with the current model (CTC greedy decoding).
• Audit each pseudo-label: pass the logits to a separate lightweight confidence
estimator (a2-layer MLP over mean-pooled encoder features, trained on the
seed set's held-out fold) and retain only utterances where estimated
confidence ≥0.9 threshold.
• Combine audited pseudo-labeled utterances with the original labeled set.

3 Phoneme-constrained augmentation — Before each training epoch, apply:

• Time stretching (0.85x–1.15x) with per-phoneme duration floor.
• Pitch shift (±2 semitones).
• Speed perturbation (0.9x–1.1x).
• Constraint: a forced-alignment phoneme recognizer (pretrained multilingual)
verifies that the augmented audio's phoneme sequence matches the original;
discard any augmentation where >20% of phonemes shift.

4 Re-train the SSL encoder + projection head from the seed checkpoint on the
combined (labeled + audited pseudo-labeled + augmented) data. Repeat for3
rounds.

Dataset / Benchmark- Primary: Common Voice (Tamil, Sinhala, Catalan, Kyrgyz —4
languages with2–8 h of validated train data each). Evaluate on each language's
official dev/test splits.

• Secondary (sanity check): FLEURS10-hour subset for2 additional languages
(Swahili, Bengali).

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | Purpose |

|---|---| | Character Error Rate (CER) | Primary metric; report mean ± std over3
seeds. | | Word Error Rate (WER) | Secondary, for languages with space-delimited
orthography. | | Pseudo-label acceptance rate | Diagnostic: % unlabeled
utterances retained per round. | | Oracle accuracy of accepted pseudo-labels |
Diagnostic: if a held-out reference exists for the unlabeled pool, measure what
fraction of accepted labels are correct. |

Report effect sizes with95% bootstrap confidence intervals across seeds.

Baselines| Baseline | Why |

|---|---| | Seed-only (fine-tune on labeled data only, no self-training) | Lower
bound — isolates the value of unlabeled data. | | Standard pseudo-labeling (no
auditing, no augmentation) | Ablates the audit mechanism. | | No-augmentation
self-training (audit + pseudo-label, no phoneme constraint) | Ablates the
augmentation contribution. | | SpecAugment self-training (SpecAugment instead of
phoneme-constrained augmentation) | Compares against a widely-used augmentation
baseline. | | wav2vec2.0 Base fine-tuned on full Common Voice (where available,
e.g., Catalan ~80 h) | Upper bound — what performance looks like with abundant
data. | | Whisper Small zero-shot | Compares against a strong multitask model
that has never seen the target language during adaptation. |

Ablations1. Audit threshold sweep — Vary the confidence threshold
(0.7,0.8,0.9,0.95) on one language to measure the precision-recall trade-off in
pseudo-label acceptance.

2 Augmentation constraint strength — Compare the phoneme-preserving constraint
against an unconstrained version (same augmentations, no phoneme-validity
check).
3 Number of self-training rounds — Compare1,2,3, and5 rounds on one language to
measure when performance plateaus or degrades.
4 Size of labeled seed — Sub-sample to1 h,2 h,5 h on a language with8 h
available, and measure whether the method's advantage grows as labeled data
shrinks.

Expected Failure Modes1. Phoneme-constraint too aggressive — The multilingual
forced-aligner may have poor accuracy on a target language it was not trained
on, causing most augmentations to be discarded. Mitigation: Relax the threshold
to40% phoneme shift tolerance; also measure the discard rate and report it.

2 Confidence estimator is poorly calibrated — On languages far from the seed
set, the auditor may either accept noisy labels (false positive) or reject
correct ones (false negative). Mitigation: Use temperature scaling (Platt
scaling) on the confidence estimator; report calibration curves (ECE) per
round.
3 Diminishing returns by round3 — The model may saturate because the unlabeled
pool's acoustic diversity is exhausted. Mitigation: If WER improvement from
round2→3 is <0.5% relative, stop early and report the saturating round as a
finding.
4 CTC beam search decoding with a weak language model — Without a
target-language n-gram or neural LM, decoding may be brittle. Mitigation: Do
not use an external LM for the main experiment (to keep the ablation clean),
but add a shallow fusion with a3-gram LM as a secondary ablation to measure
the orthogonal gain.
5 Hardware constraints — Self-training with augmentation on the full unlabeled
pool (typically50–200 h per language) may be slow. Mitigation: Downsample the
unlabeled pool to20 h per language via random sampling, stratified by speaker
if speaker metadata is available.

**1. Title**
Cross-Lingual Adapter Tuning on Discrete Phonetic Units for Ultra-Low-Resource ASR.

**2. Problem and Motivation**
Fine-tuning massive self-supervised learning (SSL) models like XLS-R or Wav2Vec 2.0 on extremely low-resource languages (e.g., <5 hours of audio) typically leads to catastrophic forgetting of the pre-trained acoustic manifold or severe overfitting. Standard fine-tuning updates millions of parameters, which is unstable with sparse gradients. There is a need for a parameter-efficient approach that leverages discrete acoustic representations to bridge the gap between continuous audio and text in data-starved scenarios.

**3. Core Hypothesis**
Integrating bottleneck adapters into a frozen multilingual SSL backbone, while utilizing discrete k-means units as intermediate targets, will yield lower Word Error Rates (WER) than standard full-parameter fine-tuning by constraining the search space and preserving pre-trained phonetic priors.

**4. Method**
*   **Backbone:** Use a frozen XLS-R (300M or 1B parameter) model as the feature extractor.
*   **Discretization:** Apply a k-means quantizer (trained on the 6th or 9th layer of the SSL model) to convert continuous latent representations into a sequence of discrete "pseudo-units."
*   **Adapter Modules:** Insert lightweight residual bottleneck adapters (rank $r=64$ or $128$) between the Transformer blocks of the encoder. Only the adapters and the final Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC) projection layer are trainable.
*   **Joint Objective:** Train using a hybrid CTC/Attention loss where the encoder is conditioned on discrete units to stabilize the alignment process before mapping to the target character/phoneme set.

**5. Dataset or Benchmark**
*   **Common Voice (v11.0):** Focus on languages with <10 hours of validated data (e.g., Swahili, Kyrgyz, Tatar, or Guarani).
*   **BABEL Development Sets:** Specifically the 1-hour and 10-hour training subsets for low-resource African and Asian languages (e.g., Zulu, Lao).

**6. Evaluation Metrics**
*   **Word Error Rate (WER):** Primary metric for transcription accuracy.
*   **Character Error Rate (CER):** To assess performance on morphologically rich or agglutinative languages.
*   **Parameter Efficiency:** Ratio of trainable parameters to total model size.

**7. Baselines**
*   **Full Fine-Tuning:** Standard XLS-R fine-tuning on the target language.
*   **Wav2Vec 2.0 + CTC:** The original Facebook AI Research (FAIR) implementation for low-resource settings.
*   **ESPnet-Transformer:** A standard E2E Transformer trained from scratch (to demonstrate the necessity of SSL).

**8. Ablations**
*   **Frozen vs. Trainable Backbone:** Testing the impact of freezing the SSL layers.
*   **Discrete vs. Continuous:** Comparing performance when using k-means units as an intermediate step versus direct audio-to-text mapping.
*   **Adapter Position:** Inserting adapters only in the upper layers versus all layers.

**9. Failure Modes and Feasibility Risks**
*   **Unit Mismatch:** Discrete units derived from a multilingual model may fail to capture unique phonemes in outlier languages (e.g., clicks or specific tonal variations).
*   **Capacity Bottleneck:** If the adapter rank is too low, the model may lack the expressivity to learn the mapping from pseudo-units to the target orthography.
*   **Computational Cost:** While parameter-efficient, the inference still requires a full pass through the large frozen backbone, which may be slow on consumer-grade hardware.

goal: Generate a research proposal on how to break the performance ceiling of small models.
answer_a_text:
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Research Proposal: Breaking the Performance Ceiling of Small Language Models via
Targeted Capacity Allocation## Title
Beyond Scaling Alone: Targeted Capacity
Allocation for Breaking the Performance Ceiling of Sub-1B Language Models

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Small language models (<1B parameters) exhibit a well-documented but
poorly understood phenomenon: diminishing returns past a critical data scale,
where additional tokens yield negligible or even negative performance gains on
held-out benchmarks. This "performance ceiling" is typically attributed to
insufficient model capacity, but recent evidence suggests that capacity is not
uniformly the bottleneck — certain capabilities (e.g., factual recall,
long-range reasoning) saturate earlier than others (e.g., syntactic fluency,
in-context pattern matching). The research problem is: Can we identify the
precise structural causes of saturation in small models and design targeted
interventions that reallocate limited capacity to the binding constraints?

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
Primary hypothesis: The performance ceiling in small models is driven
by capacity-competition between world-knowledge memorization and compositional
reasoning pathways, not by a global lack of parameters. When a small model
saturates, additional training data primarily overfits its already-congested
feedforward memory (FFN layers) while the attention-based compositional routing
remains underutilized.

Secondary hypothesis: A structured intervention that decouples these two
functions — compressing factual knowledge into a fixed, non-parametric memory
(retrieval augmentation with a small bottleneck) and freeing FFN parameters for
compositional reasoning — will raise the ceiling by10–20% on reasoning-heavy
benchmarks while matching or exceeding baselines on factual recall.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
The proposal has three stages:

Stage1: Ceiling CharacterizationTrain a350M-parameter decoder-only transformer
on increasing data scales (50M,100M,250M,500M,1B,2B,5B,10B tokens). At each
checkpoint, measure per-capability saturation curves across five categories:
factual recall, syntactic well-formedness, short-range reasoning (2 hops),
long-range reasoning (5+ hops), and in-context learning. Use influence functions
and representation similarity (CKA between hidden states at different data
scales) to identify which layers/modules saturate first and correlate with which
capability.

Stage2: Bottleneck DiagnosisInsert capacity probes — lightweight linear
classifiers at each layer that predict whether a given capability fires — to
identify the specific (layer, module) pairs where representation collision
occurs. The hypothesis is that mid-to-late FFN layers become the bottleneck for
factual recall while lower attention layers saturate for compositional
reasoning.

Stage3: Targeted Capacity AllocationIf the diagnosis confirms the hypothesis,
intervene by:

• Retrieval-Augmented Distillation (RAD): Compress the factual knowledge stored
in FFN layers into a small external memory (a frozen key-value store with ~4K
slots). Shrink the model's FFN hidden dimension by25–40% and retrain from
scratch, relying on retrieval for factual queries and freeing FFN capacity
for reasoning.
• Optional control arm: Compare against a naive "bigger FFN" baseline (same
total parameters, no retrieval) to confirm that how capacity is allocated
matters more than how much.

If the diagnosis contradicts the hypothesis (e.g., attention is the bottleneck),
pivot to attention head pruning + reallocation — removing redundant heads to
increase per-head dimensionality.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark- Training: A deduplicated, controlled-quality mix of C4
(natural language), MathPile (math/reasoning), and a synthetic factual QA
dataset (Wiki-QA, ~2M question-answer pairs with provenance). All tokenized with
the same tokenizer to avoid confounds.

• Evaluation (4 benchmarks):
• Factual recall: NaturalQuestions, TriviaQA (exact match)
• Short reasoning: BigBench-Hard subset (boolean expressions, causal judgment)
• Long reasoning: GSM8K (grade-school math, multi-step), HotpotQA (multi-hop
retrieval)
• In-context learning: MMLU (5-shot)
• Saturation diagnosis: Custom probe tasks —500 hand-written examples per
capability with controlled difficulty levels.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | Rationale |

|--------|-----------| | Accuracy (per benchmark) | Primary capability-level
metric | | Saturation threshold (η) | The data scale (in tokens) at which
performance plateaus within1% of final value | | Representation Collapse Score
(RCS) | Average pairwise CKA similarity >0.95 between adjacent data-scale
checkpoints in bottleneck layers — a proxy for when representations stop
differentiating | | Parameter-Utilization Efficiency (PUE) | Per-point
improvement per million train tokens normalized by model size; captures
diminishing returns | | Retrieval Hit Rate (RAD variant only) | Fraction of
queries where the external memory returns the correct factual document |

Primary success signal: RAD variant achieves >10% relative improvement on GSM8K
and HotpotQA over the350M baseline at the same total parameter budget, without
regressing more than2% on NaturalQuestions.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines1. Standard350M decoder (no intervention) — the ceiling-establishing
baseline2. 350M with increased FFN dimension (+25% FFN, -25% attention heads,
same total params) — tests whether naive capacity reallocation achieves similar
gains3. 350M with vanilla RAG (retrieval + standard model, no capacity
reduction) — tests whether retrieval helps regardless of capacity rebalancing4.
Distilled350M from a7B teacher (knowledge distillation alone) — tests whether
the ceiling is a training limitation vs. architectural5. 550M standard decoder
(more parameters entirely) — the "just scale up" ceiling comparison---

Ablations1. RAD without FFN shrinkage — does retrieval help when FFN capacity is
not freed?

2 RAD with different memory sizes (2K,4K,8K slots) — sensitivity to memory
bottleneck3. RAD applied at different layers (early vs. mid vs. late FFN) —
where is compressed storage most effective?
3 Retrieval-free control — train the shrunken-FFN model without retrieval;
isolates whether the gain comes from the architecture change or the
retrieval5. Ceiling characterization on a different architecture (e.g., a350M
MoE with same total params) — is the ceiling mechanism architecture-specific?

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes| Failure Mode | Mitigation / Response |

|---|---| | No clear bottleneck emerges (all modules saturate simultaneously) |
The pluralistic-ceiling hypothesis fails. Fallback: test if training recipe (LR
schedule, weight decay) is the real ceiling — ablate optimizer settings. | | RAD
improves reasoning but kills factual recall >2% | Memory size was too small.
Re-run with16K slots or use a learned gating mechanism to route queries. | |
Naive FFN-increase baseline matches or beats RAD | Capacity allocation is not
the bottleneck; the ceiling is truly total-parameter-limited. Concede and report
the negative result as a contribution (important for the community). | | No
ceiling observed (performance continues scaling linearly at10B tokens) | The350M
model was too large for the data scales tested. Scale up to50B tokens or test
a100M model to find the ceiling. | | RAD improves only on seen-document queries
(memorization, not generalization) | Evaluate on held-out timestamps and topics.
If gains vanish, the retrieval store is overfitting to the training set.
Introduce a stricter train/test split on documents. | | CKA-based diagnosis is
inconclusive | Supplement with probing classifiers and leave-one-out accuracy
drops to cross-validate which layers matter for each capability. |

**1. Title**
Recursive Latent-Space Distillation (RLSD): Enhancing Small Language Model Reasoning via Hierarchical Teacher-Trace Alignment.

**2. Problem and Motivation**
Small Language Models (SLMs) under 3B parameters consistently hit a performance ceiling in complex reasoning tasks (e.g., MATH, GSM8K) compared to large-scale models (>70B). Current distillation methods primarily focus on output-layer logit matching or simple supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on Teacher-generated Chain-of-Thought (CoT) data. However, SLMs often lack the internal "representational capacity" to mirror the teacher's logical jumps, leading to "hallucinated reasoning" where the model generates a correct format but incorrect logic. The bottleneck is not just the output, but the lack of structured intermediate latent representations that support multi-step inference.

**3. Core Hypothesis**
By aligning the SLM’s intermediate hidden states with a compressed, projection-mapped version of a Teacher model’s attention manifolds during CoT generation, the SLM can learn the *structural dependencies* of reasoning rather than just the surface-level text. This "Latent-Space Distillation" will allow a <2B parameter model to surpass the performance of a 7B model on logic-dense benchmarks.

**4. Method**
*   **Teacher Model:** Use Llama-3-70B-Instruct or GPT-4 (via API) to generate high-quality CoT traces for a reasoning dataset.
*   **Student Model:** Initialize with Phi-3-mini (3.8B) or TinyLlama-1.1B.
*   **Hierarchical Alignment:**
    1.  **Trace Extraction:** Extract hidden states and attention heads from the Teacher at specific "reasoning nodes" (defined by punctuation or logical connectors like "therefore").
    2.  **Projection Layer:** Implement a learnable linear projection layer ($W_p$) that maps the Student’s lower-dimensional hidden states ($h_s$) to the Teacher’s manifold ($h_t$).
    3.  **Loss Function:** Define a multi-objective loss:
        $L = L_{CE} + \alpha L_{MSE}(W_p h_s, h_t) + \beta L_{KLD}(A_s, A_t)$,
        where $L_{CE}$ is standard cross-entropy, $L_{MSE}$ is the latent alignment loss, and $L_{KLD}$ is the Kullback–Leibler divergence between Student ($A_s$) and Teacher ($A_t$) attention maps.
*   **Recursive Refinement:** Train in two stages: first on general knowledge, then a second pass specifically on the "failure cases" identified by the student during the first pass.

**5. Dataset or Benchmark**
*   **Reasoning:** GSM8K (Grade school math) and MATH (Harder competition math).
*   **Code:** MBPP (Mostly Basic Python Problems).
*   **General:** MMLU (Massive Multitask Language Understanding) to ensure no catastrophic forgetting of general knowledge.

**6. Evaluation Metrics**
*   **Pass@1 Accuracy:** Standard accuracy on reasoning tasks.
*   **Reasoning Fidelity:** A metric measuring the overlap between the Student’s CoT steps and the Teacher’s CoT steps using BLEU/ROUGE on intermediate steps.
*   **Efficiency Ratio:** Performance gain per million parameters compared to the baseline.

**7. Baselines**
*   **Vanilla SFT:** Training the SLM on the same CoT data without latent alignment.
*   **TinyLlama-1.1B / Phi-3-mini:** Base models without specialized distillation.
*   **Knowledge Distillation (KD):** Standard logit-based KD (e.g., using the DistilBERT approach applied to LLMs).

**8. Ablations**
*   **No Latent Alignment:** Removing the $L_{MSE}$ term to test if the projection layer is necessary.
*   **No Attention Matching:** Removing the $L_{KLD}$ term to see if attention structure matters more than hidden state values.
*   **Teacher Scaling:** Using a 7B teacher vs. a 70B teacher to measure the impact of teacher quality on latent mapping.

**9. Failure Modes and Feasibility Risks**
*   **Dimensionality Mismatch:** The gap between a 70B model’s hidden size (e.g., 8192) and an SLM’s (e.g., 2048) may be too wide for a linear projection to capture meaningful nuance, leading to "noise injection."
*   **Overfitting to Teacher Biases:** The student may inherit the specific linguistic quirks or systematic errors of the teacher model.
*   **Computational Cost:** Extracting and storing hidden states for billions of tokens is storage-intensive; this may require "on-the-fly" distillation, which increases training time by 2-3x.

Research Proposal: Compositional Reasoning Under Distraction — When Do Agentic
Workflows Break Down?

Title**"Plan-Trace-Verify: A Controlled Study of Multi-Step Compositional
Reasoning in LLM Agents Under Distractor Conditions"**

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
LLM-based agents today are deployed on tasks that require chaining
multiple reasoning steps (e.g., "book a flight, check the weather at the
destination, then find restaurants within budget"). These agents frequently fail
not because individual steps are hard, but because they lose the thread when
intermediate results contradict expectations or when irrelevant context
(distractors) is injected mid-trajectory.

The core problem: existing benchmarks evaluate reasoning in clean, single-turn
settings (e.g., GSM8K, MATH, HotpotQA), but agentic reasoning involves iterative
plan-trace cycles where earlier outputs become inputs to later steps. We lack a
controlled benchmark that isolates the effect of "distractor injection" —
irrelevant or misleading intermediate observations — on compositional reasoning
accuracy.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
H₁ (Primary): Injecting task-irrelevant but semantically plausible
observations mid-trajectory degrades LLM agent compositional reasoning accuracy
by ≥25% relative to the no-distractor baseline, even when the underlying
reasoning path is unchanged.

H₂ (Mechanism): The degradation is primarily driven by retrieval interference
(the agent attends to distractor tokens in subsequent reasoning steps) rather
than plan corruption (the agent incorrectly revises its plan). This implies that
improving selective attention (e.g., structured memory) will help more than
improving planning ability.

H₃ (Mitigation): A simple Plan-Trace-Verify loop — where the agent explicitly
writes down its plan before execution, traces each step against the plan after
receiving observations, and verifies consistency before proceeding — recovers
≥80% of the performance gap relative to the no-distractor baseline.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
### Framework: Plan-Trace-Verify (PTV)

We define three agent strategies to compare:

1 Direct-ReAct (baseline): Standard ReAct-style agent — thinks, acts, observes
in a flat loop with no explicit plan tracking.
2 Plan-then-Execute (ablation control): The agent writes a plan (as pseudocode
or bullet points) before execution, then follows it linearly, but does not
re-check consistency after each observation.
3 Plan-Trace-Verify (PTV) (proposed): The agent:

• Plan: Writes an explicit, numbered plan with preconditions and expected
postconditions for each step.
• Trace: After each observation, appends a structured trace entry: [Step N]
expected=<...> observed=<...> match=<yes|no>.
• Verify: Before the next step, runs a consistency check. If match=no, the
agent must decide: (a) proceed (the mismatch is benign), (b) re-plan from
this state, or (c) request clarification.

Distractor Injection ProtocolFor each task, we construct three conditions:

• Clean: Standard trajectory, no distractors.
• Weak distractors: One irrelevant observation per task, semantically related
to the domain but logically unnecessary (e.g., a flight search returns "Did
you know? Economy seats have30-inch pitch." between steps).
• Strong distractors: Two to three irrelevant observations, written to
plausibly contradict an intermediate expectation without actually
invalidating the correct path (e.g., a weather lookup returns "Rain expected"
when the correct reasoning only needs temperature).

Distractors are inserted at fixed positions (after step1, after step2) to ensure
controlled comparison.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark
We construct CompAgent-Distract, a synthetic multi-step
compositional reasoning dataset with500 tasks spanning three domains:

Domain                    Example Task                 Steps  Distractor Slots
Travel planning           "Book the cheapest flight    4–6    After steps1,3
to a city with population
<1M and good hiking
within50km"
Scientific literature QA  "Find the paper that         3–5    After step2
introduced method X, check
if it was published
before2020, and list its
citations that also use
dataset Y"
Multi-hop tool use        "Get the current time in     4–5    After steps1,2
Tokyo, convert to UTC, find
a meeting slot that works
for a New York participant"

Each task has:

• A gold answer (deterministic)
• A correct reasoning trace (verifiable by exhaustive enumeration)
• One clean + two distractor variants (weak, strong) -3 random seeds for
distractor surface form variationWe also evaluate on AgentQA (a subset of200
multi-turn agent tasks) for out-of-distribution generalization.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | Definition | Primary? |

|---|---|---| | Step-level accuracy | Fraction of reasoning steps where the
correct action/observation is selected given the history | Yes | | Final answer
accuracy | Exact-match (or programmatic equivalence) of the final output | Yes |
| Plan deviation rate | Fraction of episodes where the agent's actions diverge
from the optimal plan (measured by trace alignment) | Secondary | | Recovery
rate | Fraction of distractor episodes where the agent corrects itself before
the final step | Secondary | | Token cost overhead | Total input + output tokens
relative to Direct-ReAct | Efficiency |

All metrics reported with95% confidence intervals (bootstrap, N=1000) across3
seeds.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines| Baseline | Description | Why |

|---|---|---| | Direct-ReAct | Flat thought-action-observation loop | Standard
minimal agent; lower bound | | Plan-then-Execute | Pre-plan, no mid-trajectory
verification | Isolates the value of verification vs planning | | ReAct +
Self-Consistency | Sample5 trajectories, majority vote final answer | Tests
whether ensembling helps with distractors | | ReAct + Reflexion | Agent
verbalizes feedback after failure | Tests whether post-hoc reflection recovers
from distractors | | GPT-4o / Claude3.5 Sonnet (zero-shot) | No ReAct, just
prompt with tools | Measures intrinsic reasoning without agent scaffolding |

All baselines use the same backend LLM (we control for model; primary
experiments use a frontier model, with a secondary pass on an open-weight model
like Llama-3-70B).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Ablations1. Distractor position: Do distractors hurt more at early vs late
steps?

2 Distractor type: Semantic distractors vs random tokens vs plausible-but-wrong
facts — which causes the most degradation?
3 Plan granularity: Does a detailed plan (per-step pre/post conditions) help
more than a brief plan (bullet list)?
4 Verification frequency: Verify after every step vs every2 steps vs
end-of-trajectory — is there a sweet spot?
5 Memory structure: Instead of PTV's trace-and-verify, use a simple scratchpad
with a "recent observations" summary — does structured memory alone match
PTV?
6 Model scale: Does the gap between PTV and Direct-ReAct shrink or grow at
larger model sizes?

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes| Failure Mode | What to Watch For | Mitigation in Design
|

|---|---|---| | PTV overhead overwhelms small models | PTV may degrade
performance on <7B models because long traces consume context and confuse the
model | Evaluate on ≥7B; report token cost; consider ablation (ablation4:
verification frequency) | | Distractors too weak to cause degradation | If
accuracy stays at90%+, the manipulation check fails | Pilot-test distractor
strength on a development set; reject distractors that cause <5% drop on3 random
runs. If needed, escalate to "adversarial distractors" written to specifically
match common LLM failure patterns | | Plan quality variance swamps the effect |
If some agents write poor plans, plan deviation may correlate with plan quality,
not distractor handling | Pre-validate plan quality: only include episodes where
the initial plan is judged correct by an automated verifier (a separate LLM call
with rubric) | | No gap between Plan-then-Execute and PTV | If verification
doesn't help, hypothesis H₃ is falsified — but H₁ and H₂ remain testable | This
is still informative: it would suggest that planning alone (without per-step
verification) suffices for distractor robustness. We would then investigate
whether the agent implicitly verifies during planning | | Recovery rate near0 |
Agents detect mismatches but do not correct | Distinguish detection vs recovery
in metric design; if detection is high but recovery low, that's a different
(useful) finding about agentic decision-making under uncertainty | | Distractor
position confounds step difficulty | Earlier steps in a task may be
systematically easier/harder | Counterbalance: permute step order for a subset
of tasks and re-run the strongest distractor condition |
